name: Bun / man bun

card.summary: A hairstyle where long hair is gathered and coiled at the crown or nape, used to show off the face and jawline while keeping long hair tidy.
card.note: Style choice; no safety data exist.

quick.overview:
A bun is a hairstyle in which hair is pulled back, twisted or braided and coiled around itself, at the crown, back of the head or nape. The man bun is the version worn by men with long hair, a topknot influenced by Asian styles that became popular in the West in the 2010s.[1]
For looks, a bun pulls hair off the face, putting the forehead, cheekbones and jaw on display, and lets men keep length without it hanging loose. Bun height carries social cues: a high bun can read as youthful, a low one as more subdued, and a messy one as relaxed.[1]
quick.how: Wearers gather hair into a coil and secure it with a hair tie, pins, clips or a stick. It needs enough length to wrap, and is often paired with an undercut or beard.[2] Position and neatness, sleek or deliberately messy, set the vibe.[1]
quick.risks: A bun is a styling choice with no described medical risks. Reception varies: the look was widely discussed as a mid-2010s trend, and it is read differently depending on height, neatness and setting.[1]

lead: A bun is a hairstyle in which hair is pulled back, twisted or braided, and coiled around itself, usually at the crown, back of the head or nape. The man bun is a topknot influenced by Asian styles that became popular among long-haired men in the Western world.[1]

People use the style to keep long hair neat and to show the face. Bun placement carries meaning: writing in The New York Times in 2017, Hannah Goldfield associated a high bun with youthfulness and a lower one with the opposite, though perceptions have shifted over time, and a messy bun is often read as relaxed.[1]

The man bun reportedly began in London around 2010, though David Beckham wore one earlier, and Google Trends interest first appeared in 2013 and rose steeply through 2015.[1] It became associated with Brooklyn hipster culture, and celebrities such as Jared Leto, Chris Hemsworth, Leonardo DiCaprio and Orlando Bloom are commonly named as wearers.[1][2]

angle.text: A bun keeps long hair controlled while putting the face on display. Wearers adjust height, tightness and neatness, and often pair it with a shaved or faded undercut and a beard.

infobox: Long hair; hair tie, pins or clips[1][2]
Topknots in China, Japan (chonmage), Korea, and the Sikh rishi knot[1]

paras: Buns can be secured with ties, pins, clips, hair sticks or a pad, and donut-shaped inserts create a fuller shape.[1] Variants include double buns (odango in Japan; space buns in English-speaking regions), the topknot, and the Sikh rishi knot, worn as a religious practice.[1] The look ranges from sleek and polished to intentionally messy, and typically needs hair of at least about six inches.[2]

Men in ancient China wore a topknot, visible on Terracotta Army figures, until the end of the Ming Dynasty in 1644, when the Qing required the queue. Korea's Joseon-era sangtu and Japan's chonmage, worn by samurai and sumo wrestlers, are other precedents.[1]

In the 2010s the secular man bun became a Western fashion statement, tied to hipster culture and gender-norm-challenging grooming. Its prominence reached sport too, with footballer Gareth Bale wearing one in a 2015 match.[1][2]

timeline.event: End of the Ming Dynasty, after which Qing rulers required the queue instead of the topknot.[1]
The man bun reportedly begins in London.[1]
Search interest rises steeply; Gareth Bale wears a bun in a match.[1]
